clusters.part_c_scenario: Priya purchases a banker's draft for Rs. 5,00,000 from Apex Bank in Hyderabad, payable to her supplier, Mehta Enterprises in Mumbai, as an advance for machinery. Before Mehta Enterprises receives the draft, Priya has a bitter dispute with them and rushes to Apex Bank demanding that they stop payment on the draft. Apex Bank refuses, stating they cannot stop a draft once issued at her request. Priya files a consumer complaint against the bank for deficiency of service in refusing to stop payment.
clusters.part_c_content:
1. Applicable Law: The legal nature of a banker's draft is that of an obligation of the bank itself, governed by the principles of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

2. Application to Facts: Priya purchased a banker's draft, which means Apex Bank is the primary debtor. Unlike a personal cheque where the drawer can issue a stop-payment order at will, a banker's draft is an irrevocable undertaking by the issuing bank to the beneficiary (Mehta Enterprises). The purchaser (Priya) has no right to countermand payment unilaterally once the draft is handed over or dispatched.

3. Counter-Argument Addressed: Priya argues that since she paid for the draft, she retains control over the funds until encashment. However, commercial law dictates that a banker's draft equates to cash equivalent; allowing unilateral stop-payment would destroy the commercial utility and credit reliability of drafts in trade.

4. Remedy/Decision: Priya's suit or complaint against Apex Bank will fail. Apex Bank acted lawfully in refusing the stop-payment request. Priya's remedy, if any, lies in a civil suit against Mehta Enterprises for breach of contract or fraud, but she cannot compel the bank to dishonor its own negotiable instrument.
clusters.part_c_trick: Draft Problem Approach: Draft = Bank's Direct Debt (No Stop-Payment for Purchaser).

clusters.topic: Role and functions of the collecting banker
clusters.cluster_title: Role and Functions of the Collecting Banker
clusters.one_line_core_idea: A collecting banker acts as an agent to receive payment of a customer's cheque, and must exercise due care and diligence to secure the vital statutory protection of Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
clusters.real_life_scenario: Rahul deposits a Rs. 50,000 account payee cheque drawn by his client into his savings account at City Bank. City Bank collects the funds from the drawer's bank and credits Rahul's account. City Bank is acting as a collecting banker.
clusters.part_a_content: A collecting banker is a bank that undertakes to collect payment of a cheque or draft on behalf of its customer from the paying banker. Unlike a paying banker who is bound to honor a customer's mandate, a collecting banker acts primarily as an agent of the customer. However, in modern banking, the collecting banker often assumes the dual character of an agent for collection and a holder for value when they permit the customer to draw against the uncleared cheque. The primary duty of a collecting banker is to present the cheque for payment within a reasonable time and to remit the proceeds to the customer. To protect themselves from liability for conversion if the customer's title to the cheque turns out to be defective, collecting bankers rely heavily on statutory protection, notably Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which shields them from conversion claims if they act in good faith and without negligence.
part_a_key_points: AGENT OF CUSTOMER — The fundamental legal character of a collecting banker is that of an agent receiving payment on behalf of the customer.
HOLDER FOR VALUE — When the banker allows a customer to withdraw funds against a cheque before clearance, the banker becomes a holder for value with independent rights.
DUTY OF CARE — The banker must present cheques within a reasonable time, observe crossing instructions, and promptly notify the customer of dishonour.
STATUTORY PROTECTION — Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides immunity from liability for conversion if collection is done in good faith and without negligence.
CONVERSION LIABILITY — Without statutory protection, a collecting banker who receives payment on a defective title cheque is liable to the true owner for the tort of conversion.
COLLECTION OF DRAFTS — The statutory immunity extends beyond cheques to include bank drafts as per amendments to the Negotiable Instruments Act.
clusters.part_a_trick: Mnemonic: ABC - Agent status, Burden of care, Collection protection under Section 131.
clusters.part_b_content: Introduction: In the modern commercial world, the collection of cheques and drafts forms a vital part of banking operations. A collecting banker is a financial institution that receives a cheque from its customer with the instruction to present it to the drawee bank and collect the proceeds. Legal Nature of Relationship: The primary legal relationship between a collecting banker and a customer is that of principal and agent. When a customer deposits a cheque for collection, the banker does not become the owner of the cheque immediately; rather, the banker undertakes to collect the money as an agent. However, this agency relationship can transform into that of a creditor and debtor if the banker allows the customer to draw against the uncollected cheque, thereby making the banker a holder for value. Duties and Responsibilities of a Collecting Banker: 1. Reasonable Diligence: The banker must present the cheque for payment within a reasonable time. Unreasonable delay that results in loss makes the banker liable. 2. Observance of Crossings: The banker must strictly adhere to the crossing instructions on the cheque. Collecting a crossed cheque improperly can strip the banker of statutory protection. 3. Notice of Dishonour: If the cheque is dishonoured, the banker must communicate the same to the customer without undue delay. 4. Collection of Account Payee Cheques: Special care must be taken with account payee cheques; crediting them to an account other than the named payee's constitutes gross negligence. Statutory Protection under Section 131: The most critical aspect of a collecting banker's legal position is the risk of conversion. If a customer deposits a stolen or forged cheque, and the collecting banker receives payment and credits the customer, the true owner of the cheque can sue the banker for the tort of conversion. To mitigate this harsh rule, Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides a statutory shield. For a banker to claim protection under Section 131, the following conditions must be met: (a) The banker must receive payment for a customer; (b) The banker must act in good faith; and (c) The banker must act without negligence. The Supreme Court and various High Courts have consistently held that opening an account without proper introduction and due diligence constitutes negligence, thereby depriving the banker of Section 131 protection. Case Laws: In the landmark case of Commissioners of Taxation v. English, Scottish and Australian Bank, the Privy Council clarified that 'negligence' under Section 131 means failure to exercise reasonable care in receiving payment, particularly in opening accounts without proper references. Similarly, in Bhimji v. Bombay Trust Corporation, the duties regarding the careful handling of crossed cheques were underscored. Conclusion: The role of the collecting banker is fraught with risks of conversion. By strictly adhering to KYC norms, exercising reasonable care in opening accounts, and following clearing instructions meticulously, a collecting banker can successfully invoke Section 131 and safeguard itself from liability.

part_b_case_laws.case_name: Commissioners of Taxation v. English, Scottish and Australian Bank
part_b_case_laws.holding: The Privy Council held that negligence under the equivalent of Section 131 requires a consideration of whether the banker's conduct disregarded the ordinary standards applied by bankers, specifically regarding account opening checks.
part_b_case_laws.trick: Think of 'Taxation Bank' failing to pay attention during account opening.

clusters.part_c_scenario: Priya steals a bearer cheque worth Rs. 1,00,000 belonging to her employer, Mehta, and deposits it into her own newly opened savings account at Apex Bank. Apex Bank collects the money from the drawee bank without making any inquiries about Priya's employment or the source of the cheque. Mehta, upon discovering the theft, sues Apex Bank for the tort of conversion.
clusters.part_c_content:
1. Applicable Law: The legal issue revolves around the liability of a collecting banker for conversion and the availability of statutory protection under Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Under common law, receiving payment on a defective title cheque constitutes conversion. Section 131 protects the banker only if it acts in good faith and without negligence.
2. Application to Facts: Apex Bank received payment for a customer (Priya). However, the crucial test is whether the bank acted without negligence. Opening an account for a new customer without proper introduction, background checks, or verifying the source of substantial funds constitutes negligence on the part of the bank.
3. Counter-Argument: Apex Bank may argue that the cheque was a bearer cheque and that they merely performed their routine collection duty as agents without actual knowledge of the theft.
4. Decision and Remedy: The argument of Apex Bank will fail. Failure to conduct basic KYC and reference checks when opening the account amounts to negligence per se. Consequently, Apex Bank is denied the protection of Section 131 and is held liable to Mehta (the true owner) for the full value of the cheque in an action for conversion.
clusters.part_c_trick: Mnemonic for Problem Questions: 'C-N-P' - Check customer identity, Note the lack of negligence, Prove statutory protection or face conversion liability.
